newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade official seeks Chinese contract for Boeing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade official seeks Chinese contract for Boeing.

text.p: Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat is heading to China to lobby for billions of dollars in potential contracts for Boeing Co. and other U.S. businesses, federal officials said Thursday.
Eizenstat will lay the groundwork for Vice President Al Gore's trip to China in late March, during which he hopes to witnessess the signing of some of those multibillion-dollar contracts.

"We're talking potentially, if you add it all up, about tens of billions of dollars," said a senior U.S. trade official. He said Eizenstat also will be talking to Chinese officials about potential contracts in telecommunications and power plants as well.
Eizenstat plans to open a U.S. commercial centre in Shanghai and meet with business leaders and top Chinese officials in Beijing. He will wind up his trip in Hong Kong.

Eizenstat said his trip, coming on the heels of this week's visit by Secretary of State Madeliene Albright, shows the importance the administration places on the U.S. relationship with China and the accelerated pace of that improving relationship.

"Although there are clear differences and disagreements between the United States and China, it is important to acknowledge that an open, prosperous, stable China integrated into the world community is in our national interest," Eizenstat said in a statement.

He said he plans to discuss a whole range of issues with Chinese officials, including human rights, nuclear technology proliferation, the handover of Hong Kong, cooperation on the Korean Peninsula and the growing U.S. trade deficit and opening markets. He said progress on those issues over the next few months will weigh heavily on support for continuing the U.S. policy of comprehensive engagement with China.

"No single issue is more important than explaining to the Chinese that continued support for U.S. engagement with China depends on the American people and the Congress seeing progress and results across a broad spectrum," he said.
Eizenstat will be in China as U.S. trade negotiators head to Geneva for talks with Chinese officials on Beijing's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.

U.S. officials are hoping to see, in writing, promises made by Chinese officials to undertake some of the reforms and remove some of the barriers the United States and other key trading partners have said are necessary for China's entry into the global trading system.

The U.S. trade deficit with China jumped 17 percent last year to nearly $40 billion, and U.S. trade officials said the key to reducing that huge imbalance is to open China's vast markets to more imports.

A U.S. trade official, who asked not to be identified, said the huge deficit and progress in China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation as well as efforts to resolve deep differences over trade in wheat and other agricultural products will be major issues in the upcoming debate on China's most favoured nation (MFN) trade status. The farm lobby has been among the most ardent supporters of such trade status for China, the official noted.
China's MFN status, which allows its goods to enter the United States at the same low tariff rates given most other trading partners, is subject to annual Congressional review.
